subsection: 2. Cultural variations and the marriage relationship

notes.b: The arrangements around marriage are not the same everywhere. They differ in who may marry, who chooses the partner and how many partners a person may have.
points: The minimum age for marriage varies between countries and cultures; in Ireland both partners must be at least 18.

In an arranged marriage, parents or families choose the spouse on the basis of background and suitability, usually with the couple's consent. This contrasts with a marriage freely chosen by the couple themselves.
Arranged marriage is traditional in some communities, for example Sikh, Japanese and Travelling communities, but not for every member of those communities.
Some cultures restrict the choice of spouse by religion, social class or kinship (family relationship), meaning a person may not marry someone from a particular group.
Monogamy, meaning one husband and one wife at a time, is the norm in Western countries, including Ireland, so one marriage at a time is also what the law there recognises.

Polygamy, meaning more than one spouse at a time, is the general term and is not permitted in Ireland. Marrying again without the death or divorce of the first spouse is bigamy, which is a criminal offence.
Polygamy has two forms: polygyny, where one man has more than one wife, and polyandry, where one woman has more than one husband.
Same-sex marriage is legal in some countries, including Ireland since the Marriage Act 2015, and not recognised in others.
notes.tip: Don't mix up polygamy (the general term) with polygyny and polyandry (its two forms), and don't say monogamy is illegal elsewhere. For 'cultural variations' questions, give each variation a short explanation, not just a label.

notes.b: The same legal marriage can be celebrated in different ways, depending on the couple's beliefs. The choice of ceremony is one more way marriage varies between people and cultures.
points: Marriage may be a civil ceremony before a registrar or a religious ceremony; both are legally valid when the marriage is registered.
Some couples choose a secular or humanist ceremony, which has no religious content.

Interfaith marriages join partners of different religions, so the couple must agree how the ceremony and their family's religious life will be arranged, for example which traditions the children will follow.
notes.tip: A question on why marriage is popular in Ireland today looks for the choice of civil or same-sex marriage, security for the couple and children, and social and legal recognition, not detailed law.

notes.b: Weddings are full of customs that carry meaning for the people who follow them. These customs differ by culture and religion, in dress, symbols, venue and the form of the ceremony.
points: Dress and symbols such as a veil and a wedding ring, and throwing rice or confetti, are wedding customs that have been popular for centuries in many cultures.
Jewish weddings are held under a canopy, which symbolises the couple's future home.
At the end of a Jewish wedding, a glass is broken under foot to recall the destruction of the ancient Temple in Jerusalem.
Quaker couples marry at a public gathering with no priest or official present, because Quakers believe God alone joins a couple as husband and wife.
The ceremony can take place in a church, mosque, synagogue, registry office or other approved location, depending on the couple's religion and the law of the country.
notes.tip: Exams ask for three or four ways customs differ, each needing a short explanation. Pick clear ones such as the veil, ring, rice throwing, venue and civil, religious or interfaith ceremony.

notes.b: Marriage is more than a private promise. It is a public commitment that carries legal obligations, and couples keep it going through how they live day to day.
points: Spouses make a public commitment to each other, usually through vows or declarations before witnesses during the ceremony, sealed by registration of the marriage.
Because marriage carries legal obligations, spouses owe each other the rights and responsibilities below, which the law can enforce.
Commitment is maintained, so that the marriage lasts, by working on the relationship, communicating positively and remaining faithful and loyal.
Commitment is also shown through sharing responsibility for the home, money and children, for example through shared finances and a shared home.

notes.b: A right is something each spouse is entitled to receive from the other because they are married. These rights are the other side of the responsibilities each partner takes on.
points: Each other's company: spouses are entitled to live together as a couple.

Sexual relations: each spouse is entitled to sexual relations with the other, and consummation is the basis of the marriage. An unconsummated marriage can be annulled (declared never to have been valid) in some circumstances.
Faithfulness: each spouse is entitled to the other's loyalty and faithfulness within a monogamous marriage, because the marriage is a promise to one partner only.
Inheritance: under the Succession Act 1965, a spouse who dies without a will (intestate) leaves the whole estate to the surviving spouse if there are no children.
If there are children and no will, the surviving spouse takes two-thirds of the estate and the children share one-third.

Legal right share: a surviving spouse can claim a share of the estate even where a will leaves them less, so a will cannot cut them out. The share is one half if there are no children and one third if there are children.
notes.tip: Name the Succession Act 1965 when you write about inheritance, because marking schemes reward the Act. In a rights-and-responsibilities answer, give two to four of each and balance them.

notes.b: Marriage also places duties on each partner, towards each other and towards their children. Some of these are backed by law and some depend on commitment.
points: Financial support: each spouse must support the other (a dependent spouse) and any dependent children. The Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976 allows a spouse to seek maintenance through the court.

Joint guardianship: married parents are both guardians of their children and share responsibility for their care and upbringing, under the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964 as amended by the Children and Family Relationships Act 2015.
Children's needs: parents must provide for their children's physical, emotional, social, moral, educational and spiritual needs.
Commitment: spouses must work on the relationship, show loyalty and keep their commitment to the marriage.
Positive communication: spouses must talk openly about decisions, finances and family matters to keep the marriage functioning.
Caring for a sick spouse is also a responsibility, since marriage means looking after your partner when they are ill.
notes.tip: Name the Maintenance Act 1976 for financial support. Cover spouse and children, joint guardianship, children's needs, commitment and communication, and caring for a sick partner.

keyTerms.definition: A marriage in which parents or families choose the spouse, based on background and suitability.
A marriage arrangement in which a person has one spouse at a time.
A marriage arrangement in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time.
A form of polygamy in which a man has more than one wife.
A form of polygamy in which a woman has more than one husband.
The offence of marrying a second time while still legally married to another person, without the first marriage having ended by death or divorce.
Sexual intercourse between the spouses after the marriage ceremony.
The shared legal right and responsibility of both parents to care for and make decisions about their child.
The person who conducts a marriage ceremony, such as a priest, minister, registrar or celebrant.

factCards.definition: The right to live together, the right to sexual relations, the right to faithfulness and loyalty, and the right to inherit from each other.
Financial support for the spouse and children, joint guardianship of the children, providing for the children's needs, and commitment to the relationship through communication.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which marriage customs or arrangements can differ between cultures.
questions.model: Any two of the following, each described: arranged marriages, where parents choose the spouse on the basis of background and suitability; restrictions on who may be chosen as a spouse by religion, social class or kinship; differences in the number of spouses allowed, such as monogamy, polygamy, polygyny or polyandry; differences in the ceremony, such as veils, rings, rice throwing, canopies, or a Quaker meeting without an officiant; differences in the age at which people may marry; same-sex marriage being recognised in some countries and not in others.

questions.prompt: Explain the rights that spouses hold towards each other and the duties they owe to their children under Irish law, and show how commitment supports both.
questions.model: Rights between spouses: the right to live together and have each other's company; the right to a sexual relationship and consummation of the marriage; the right to faithfulness and loyalty within a monogamous marriage; the right to inherit, under the Succession Act 1965, the whole estate with no will and no children, or two-thirds with children, and a legal right share even where a will provides less. Duties to children: financial support for the spouse and children under the Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976; joint guardianship, with shared responsibility for care and upbringing; a legal duty to provide for the children's physical, emotional, social, moral and educational needs. Commitment: spouses show commitment by working on the relationship, communicating openly and sharing finances, a home and parenting, which allows both rights and responsibilities to be honoured over the life of the marriage.
